theme: “Great is your faithfulness”, hope in the midst of suffering
readingInstruction: Read Lamentations 3:1-66. This is the center of the book, a long poem in which the poet moves from despair to a stunning declaration of hope. Read verses 19 to 33 slowly. They are the heart of the book.
settingTheScene: Chapter 3 is the only chapter in which the speaker is an individual, “the man who has seen affliction.” It is a triple acrostic, in which three verses in a row begin with each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, making 66 verses. Its structure of increasing order is placed over its disorder. At the center, the poet speaks of hope in the middle of suffering.
observation: “I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath” (v. 1).
“He has driven and brought me into darkness without any light” (v. 2).
“He has besieged me and surrounded me with bitterness and tribulation” (v. 5).
“So I say, My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD” (v. 18).
“But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope” (v. 21).
“The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (vv. 22-23).
“The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him” (v. 24).
“For he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men” (v. 33).
interpretation:
The chapter opens in complete darkness. The speaker catalogs his suffering: God has walled him in, bound him with heavy chains, shut out his prayer, made his path crooked. He is like a bear or a lion lying in wait. The images are of a person who feels that God himself has become his enemy. And he reaches the bottom in verse 18: “My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD.”

Then comes the hinge: “But this I call to mind.” The word “call to mind” means to bring back to the heart. He does not argue himself out of his pain. He remembers something. And what he remembers is the character of God. “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.”

This is among the best known passages in Lamentations, and it is worth noting where it appears: in the center of the book of grief, in the aftermath of the destruction of Jerusalem. These are not words from a place of comfort. They are words from the ashes. The faithfulness of God is great precisely when everything else is gone.

The poet continues: “The LORD is my portion… therefore I will hope in him.” He has lost everything but has God. It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. It is good to bear the yoke in youth. God’s discipline is not endless: “Though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love.” And he adds a statement that gives light to everything: “He does not afflict from his heart.” Judgment is God’s “strange work.” His heart is mercy.

The rest of the chapter returns to prayer and to a plea for justice. But the poem has made its point: hope is a decision to remember who God is.
connection: Hebrews 4:15-16 says we have a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses. 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 says we are afflicted but not crushed. Hebrews 12:5-11 explains that the Lord disciplines the one he loves. Romans 5:3-5 says that suffering produces endurance, character, and hope. Isaiah 53:3 describes Jesus as a man of sorrows. The hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” is based on verses 22 and 23.
application:
Start each day this week by saying, “His mercies are new every morning.”

Think of a time of affliction when you remembered something about God that gave you hope. Write it down.

Wait quietly before God for a few minutes, as verse 26 teaches.
prayerPrompts: Tell God how weary you are.
Call to mind his steadfast love and mercies, and name one.
Tell him you wait for him because he is good.
